title: Standardization of Post-Publication Code Verification is Possible with the Support of the Community
claim: Reproducibility requirements across venues concentrate at submission, leaving almost no verification at later stages, especially after publication.
layout: Single matrix: venues as rows, lifecycle stages as columns, legend top-right
description: A timeline matrix of reproducibility policies. Rows are grouped into Journals (AIJ, DMLR, JAIR, TMLR, TPAMI and others), Conferences (AAAI, CVPR, ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS and others) and ACM-affiliated venues (EuroSys, PPoPP, SIGIR). Columns are publication stages: Submission, Review, Acceptance, Publication and Post-publication, marked by dotted vertical guides. Each venue has a horizontal blue line. Black-and-white symbols mark where policies apply. Open circles mean code/data is encouraged, filled and double circles mean required, squares mean artifact evaluation, and open and filled stars mean independent reproduction and replication. A boxed legend sits at the top right, and footnotes with asterisks sit below. Nearly all symbols cluster in the Submission column. A few ACM venues have marks at Review or Acceptance, and ICLR and NeurIPS have marks at Post-publication. The Post-publication column is mostly empty, which is the gap the paper highlights.
caption: Reproducibility policies in journals, conferences and ACM-affiliated venues.
abstract: Reproducibility remains a challenge in machine learning research. While code and data availability requirements have become increasingly common, post-publication verification is still limited and unformalized. This position paper argues that journals and conference proceedings should all implement a post-publication verification submission system. We propose a modification to ACM and IEEE Access verification badges that allows independent researchers to submit post-publication code replications directly to the journal or proceedings, leading to visible verification badges included in the article metadata. Each article may earn up to two badges, each linked to verified code in its corresponding public repository. This framework would be a step forward toward a standardized reproducibility policy and would provide young researchers with an opportunity to improve their curriculum. We describe the motivation, related initiatives, a formal framework, the potential impact, possible limitations, and alternative views.
